articles.title: Godot save files lie about their format - sniff the content, not the extension
articles.excerpt: In Godot 4, the most-used save addon on GitHub writes a file called save_data.sav. It is plain JSON. That is not a bug. It is a naming choice, and it is fine for the game. It breaks every other progra…
articles.body: In Godot 4, the most-used save addon on GitHub writes a file called save_data.sav . It is plain JSON. That is not a bug. It is a naming choice, and it is fine for the game. It breaks every other program that touches the file - an external editor, a debug script, a CI check, or a coding agent - as soon as that program decides the file format from the extension. What the file actually is SaveMadeEasy (220+ stars, MIT) is the Godot 4 save/load addon you find first when you search for one. In its source, the default path is const default_file_path : = "user://save_data.sav" and it writes with file . store_string ( JSON . stringify ( current_state_dictionary , " \t " )) Encryption is off by default.

articles.title: Your AI agent just did something it shouldn't. Here's the first hour.
articles.excerpt: Picture the message in your team chat: "Why did the support bot email a customer's invoice to an address nobody recognizes?" If your agent can call tools, this will happen to you in some form. It migh…
articles.body: Picture the message in your team chat: "Why did the support bot email a customer's invoice to an address nobody recognizes?" If your agent can call tools, this will happen to you in some form. It might be a prompt injection, a model misreading an instruction, or a leaked key. Most incident response plans were written for servers and phishing. They don't say what to do when the thing that misbehaved is a language model holding your credentials. Here is the order of operations I use. Most of it comes down to one rule: contain first, understand later. Before anything happens: four things to build now You can't improvise these during an incident. A kill switch. One action that disables a single tool, or the whole agent, without a deploy. Test it the way you'd test a backup restore.

articles.title: Give Claude Code a real browser with Playwright MCP
articles.excerpt: Claude Code can write a login form, but it cannot see whether the form works. Give it a real browser and it can open the page, click through, and tell you what broke. Playwright MCP is Microsoft's Mod…
articles.body: Claude Code can write a login form, but it cannot see whether the form works. Give it a real browser and it can open the page, click through, and tell you what broke. Playwright MCP is Microsoft's Model Context Protocol server that does exactly this. Instead of screenshots, it hands the model Playwright's accessibility tree: a structured text view of the page. That means no vision model is needed, and actions are more deterministic than clicking at pixel coordinates. Our shorter how-to is on the Deduped use-case page . Here is the full setup.

articles.title: Cut Claude Code token spend with Headroom: a 5 step setup
articles.excerpt: Claude Code gets expensive for a boring reason: most of what it reads is noise. Test logs, JSON tool output, long diffs and old conversation turns all go back to the model on every step, and you pay f…
articles.body: Claude Code gets expensive for a boring reason: most of what it reads is noise. Test logs, JSON tool output, long diffs and old conversation turns all go back to the model on every step, and you pay for each token again. Headroom is an open source tool that sits between your agent and the model and compresses that material before it is sent. According to its README, a log that costs 10,144 tokens can shrink to 1,260 while the same fatal error is still found. Compression runs on your machine, and the originals are cached locally so the model can ask for the full text when it needs it. This is a practical walkthrough for Claude Code. Our longer write-up of the same setup is on the Deduped use-case page .

Choice Retrieval quality Latency control Operational fit Staged retrieval with explicit collections Measurable against expected sources Each stage gets its own bound Best default for a small team shipping weekly One broad vector query Easy to start, harder to diagnose One limit and timeout Fine for a narrow, clean corpus Search every source at request time Fresh by construction A slow source can hold up the answer Better when indexing is unacceptable Short answer: use staged retrieval, explicit collections, bounded queries, traceable source context, and a 25-question labeled evaluation set before production rollout.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 28, 1971: Britain launches its 1st satellite Prospero into space on a Black Arrow rocket
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 28, 1971, the United Kingdom launched its first satellite. The satellite was named Prospero, but it was also known as the X-3. This wasn't Britain's first satellite , but it was the first and only one the British space program launched with one of its own rockets. The first six British satellites all launched from the United States on NASA rockets. Prospero launched on a carrier rocket called the Black Arrow. The Prospero mission was the fourth and final flight of a Black Arrow rocket . Prospero was designed to study how the environment in space affects communications satellites. It tested things solar cells and telemetry systems, and even had a micrometeoroid detector that would determine small particles in space posed a threat to the spacecraft.

articles.title: 5 days beneath the waves: What it's like to live in an underwater 'space station'
articles.excerpt: Confined inside a research station 22 feet (7 meters) underwater, Analog Astronaut Commander Dr. Musilova and her crew performed research and maintenance activities like future astronauts on Mars.
articles.body: Living underwater was surprisingly peaceful. It was in many ways exactly what I imagine living on Mars would be like one day. There were no humans around us, except for my three SEA STAR crewmembers and me. Apart from the human noises we made, we couldn't hear anything other than the life support systems keeping us alive submerged 22 feet (7 meters) below the surface. We were living in these extreme conditions to study the challenges astronauts may face on long-duration space missions. Since performing research in space is still rare and expensive, there are numerous facilities around the world that focus on recreating space-like conditions on Earth . One of those stations is the Jules' Undersea Lab, where the SEA STAR simulated space mission took place.

articles.title: ISS astronaut will conduct Canada's 1st spacewalk in 7 years on Oct. 29: Watch it live
articles.excerpt: Joshua Kutryk will venture outside the International Space Station on Oct. 29, on the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut in more than seven years. Here's how to watch it live.
articles.body: The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years. Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force . The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com , courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

articles.title: Meet Apeiron, Virgin Galactic's 1st 'Delta-class' space plane
articles.excerpt: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled its first "Delta-class" space plane, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.
articles.body: Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name. Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents. The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.
